groundTruthNarrative: The Tarrant Valley Symphony's 30% ticket-revenue decline is not a management failure. Almost all of it came in one step in 2023-24, the first season after Castellan Hall closed and concerts moved to Brightwater, a venue with 40% fewer seats, poor evening transit and $24 parking. Single-ticket sales fell 45% that year against a 9% peer median, and the share of subscribers who rarely attended doubled. Downtown cathedral concerts in the same seasons, at the same prices and with similar repertoire, sold about 50% more, which works as a natural experiment. Lapsed patrons name access far more often than programming. Comparable orchestras that never moved lost 25-35% over the same period, so the size of the decline is ordinary for the region. Committed subscribers renew at a steady 85-86%, and concerts with modern works sell no worse than those without, so the programming story fails. Marketing's effect cannot be judged without attribution data, and whether revenue would have fallen less in the old hall is unknowable from this evidence. Dropping the music director would forfeit $400k a year and punish the wrong party.

answers.rationale: Timing does not fit: revenue fell 28.5% in 2023-24, when the post-1945 share rose only from 18% to 21%, then held roughly flat (+1.4%, -3.4%) while the share rose to 27% and 31% (E2, E6). In the same venue, concerts with substantial modern works sold slightly more than those without (1,034 vs 1,019, E7). Cathedral concerts with comparable repertoire sold 1,520 (E11). Peers that did not change venue lost a similar cumulative share (E10), so the total is explicable without any programming effect. The complaint emails and press column (E3) are self-selected anecdotes with no concert-level data. Programming cannot be the main cause.

The orchestra's cumulative decline was -29.9% (E2). Six comparable orchestras declined by -25% to -35% over the same seasons, median -29% (E10). The decline sits at the regional median, so its size alone is no sign of orchestra-specific underperformance. The claim is about magnitude only and does not depend on what caused the peer decline.

The move happened before 2023-24 (E9). Single-ticket sales fell 45% that season against a 9% peer median (E4, E10). The share of subscribers attending 0-2 concerts doubled from 14% to 29%, and their renewal fell from 60% to 43% (E5). The mechanism is documented: last bus at 22:10, rail 2.4 km away, $24 parking (E9). Lapsed patrons name travel, parking/safety or seat availability 67% of the time against 11% for programming (E12). Downtown cathedral concerts in the same seasons and price bands sold 1,520 against 1,027, with single-ticket buyers making up 58% of sales (E11). Timing, mechanism, covariation and a within-season comparison together support the claim.

The only evidence that marketing was ineffective is the chair's assertion (E1). Spend was flat (E16), and there was a three-month vacancy (E14), but the organization has never tracked which campaigns sell tickets. Both the ED and the marketing director say they cannot judge effectiveness (E14, E16). Nothing in the case shows marketing helped or hurt, so the claim is live but unestablished. It is also not the music director's responsibility (E13).

Subscribers who attend 3 or more concerts renewed at 85-86% in every season, including those when modern repertoire rose most (E5, E6). Losses are concentrated among low-usage subscribers, whose share jumped at the venue move rather than with the repertoire shift (E5). One might argue that dissatisfied subscribers would simply attend less and move into that group. The exit survey counters this: only 11% of lapsed patrons cite programming (E12), and only 12% of current patrons who attend less name it (E8). The mixed satisfaction figures (E8) do not show defection.

This is a counterfactual about the whole three-season total, and the evidence points both ways. Peers that never moved still lost a median 29% (E10), which suggests a large decline would have happened anyway. But the orchestra outperformed peers before the move (+6% vs +1%) and stayed nearly flat after it while peers fell about 22% (E2, E10). That pattern fits either an audience that was more resilient (so a smaller decline in the old hall) or a venue shock that front-loaded losses peers took gradually. The return intentions in E12 are stated, not observed. The venue effect on single tickets is established (I3), but how much the total would have changed without the move cannot be determined here (see Q2).

Temporal order: single-ticket sales fell 45% in the first season at Brightwater (E4, E9). Covariation beyond the regional trend: peers fell 9% (E10). Mechanism: the transit and parking barriers (E9) are the main lapse reasons (E12). Natural experiment: the same orchestra, prices and repertoire mix at a downtown venue in the same seasons sold about 50% more, with a much higher single-ticket share (E11). The programming rival is ruled out by E7. Together these meet the standard for a causal link.

On the surface both trends move together over four seasons, which is the trap. Year by year they diverge: the large revenue drop coincided with a small repertoire change, and the largest repertoire increases coincided with flat revenue (E2, E6). Within the same venue and seasons, concerts with substantial modern works sold no worse (E7), and modern-work programs at the cathedral sold well (E11). The evidence counts against the link, so the answer is contradicted rather than association-only.

Prices rose ($46.80 to $50.00 to $54.00) while tickets per concert fell (E2), so the two co-occur. The price rises coincided with the capacity cut and venue move (E9) and with a regional decline in which peers also raised prices about 14% (E10). The ED explicitly says the effects cannot be separated (E14). No price test or elasticity evidence is supplied, so causation is not established.

Non-renewal on revenue grounds punishes the wrong party. The decline is explained by the venue move and the regional trend (E10, E11), the programming link is contradicted (E7), and the music director has no marketing responsibility (E13). It would also trigger the key-person clause and forfeit $400,000 a season in Halvorsen funding (E15), about a quarter of current ticket revenue. The outcome is a likely net worsening, not merely an early commitment, so the answer is harmful rather than premature.

The board faces an irreversible decision by 31 December 2026 (E13), based on a narrative the evidence contradicts (E1 against E4, E5, E7, E10, E11). Putting the segmented analysis in front of the board and separating any artistic judgment from the revenue question directly prevents the harmful action. It costs little, and the data already exists.

This targets the established causal mechanism (I3, I7). The cathedral concerts are proven in these seasons to sell about 50% more and contribute about $31,000 more per concert (E11), and six dates are on offer. The shuttle addresses the documented last-bus gap (E9) that lapsed patrons cite (E12). It is reversible, limited to the interim season left by the delay to September 2027 (E9), and backed by direct evidence.

Replacing the outside agency (E16) and restructuring the team would be justified only if marketing ineffectiveness (H4) were confirmed. Without attribution data the case cannot establish that (E14, E16), and the marketing director has been in post only since September 2024. Nothing shows the restructuring would worsen outcomes, so it is premature rather than harmful. Q1 would resolve the question.

Dropping commissions breaks the condition of the $180,000-a-season State Arts Council grant, which requires two or more commissions or premieres (E15). The evidence shows no sales penalty for modern works (E7, E11) to offset that loss. The survey preference for familiar classics (41%) is matched by 59% who want the current balance or more new work (E8). The action means a certain loss for no expected gain.

The evidence establishes a causal venue effect with a within-season natural experiment (E11), a timed step change against peers (E4, E10) and a documented mechanism (E9, E12). That is enough to commit to the venue-mitigation intervention (A3), which is reversible and shown to pay for itself. Open questions (H4, H6) do not block it. The evidence is not sufficient to justify the board's proposed intervention, but the question asks about a substantive intervention in general.
